terra.problem: “They unpacked” is a flat punchline where the move could make room for a stronger laugh.
Abram is introduced without saying who he is.
The joke makes the number of names in the chapter, and thus the way Scripture is written, its target.
The explanation says nobody is throwing a parade and somebody is restocking shelves. The passage says neither.
“She just blessed them” recasts Naomi's words. She tells them, “May the LORD…” rather than the text saying she blessed them.
The explanation presents Ruth's promise as a certainty that distance will not separate them, rather than as what Ruth said.
The out-walking joke appears on a card about death. Heavy moments have no joke.
Saying the town's eyes are on Naomi adds a detail the text doesn't give. The whole town is stirred because of both Naomi and Ruth.

explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Ruth 1:1 says the family went to reside in the land of Moab, and verse 2 says they entered Moab and settled there. They didn't just pass through. They unpacked.

Egypt is a smart guess, friend, because Abram once went down to Egypt during a famine too (Genesis 12:10). But this family heads somewhere else. Ruth 1:1 says they went to live in the land of Moab. Same problem, different map.

Edom is the name the Bible gives Esau and his family line (Genesis 36:1, 9). But Elimelech's family isn't headed there, baker. Ruth 1:1 says they went to reside in the land of Moab. Verse 2 says they settled there.

There she is, baker. Ruth 1:4 says the sons married Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. She just walked into the story, and the whole book carries her name. Keep your eye on this one.

Rachel is a big name in Genesis, friend, but she's Jacob's wife (Genesis 29:28). The second Moabite woman here is Ruth, says Ruth 1:4. Totally different family tree. Easy to mix up when the names start coming fast.

Dinah shows up way back in Genesis as Jacob's daughter (Genesis 30:21). The Moabite woman here is Ruth (Ruth 1:4). I'll give you this, baker, there are a LOT of names in this chapter. Elimelech, Mahlon, Chilion, Orpah, it's like your first day at a new job when everybody introduces themselves at once.
Yes, baker. Ruth 1:5 says both Mahlon and Chilion also died. Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband. That's a lot of loss for one family, and the chapter doesn't rush past it.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything happened to her house, friend. Ruth 1:5 says both of her sons, Mahlon and Chilion, died. Her husband Elimelech was already gone (Ruth 1:3), so now Naomi is left without all three of them. That's the heartbreak this verse is about.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Ruth 1:5 doesn't say Naomi got sick or lost her sight, baker. It says both of her sons died. Now she has lost her husband and her two boys. I think that's about as heavy as it gets.

Right on, baker. Ruth 1:6 says Naomi heard that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food. This whole story kicked off with a famine (Ruth 1:1), so this is the news she needed. That's the kind of news that gets you up off the couch.

No king in this news, friend. This story is set in the days when the judges ruled (Ruth 1:1). Ruth 1:6 says the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food. After a famine, that's the headline.

No battle news here, baker. Ruth 1:6 says the LORD provided His people with food. The chapter started with a famine back home (Ruth 1:1), so food is the big story. Nobody's throwing a parade, but somebody's restocking the shelves.

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. In Ruth 1:8, Naomi says, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” They're already out on the road with her, and she turns around and sends them home. I bet that was not an easy thing to say.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't timing the trip, friend. In Ruth 1:8 she says, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” Nothing about racing the sunset. She's more like a GPS that keeps saying 'make a U-turn' no matter how far you drive.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: It's actually the opposite, baker. In Ruth 1:8, Naomi says, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” She's sending them away, not pulling them closer. Picture helping somebody move, and halfway down the highway they tell you to turn the truck around and go home.

True, baker. In Ruth 1:9, Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” She's wishing them a whole new start. I think even in her own grief, she's thinking about their future.

It's actually true, friend. In Ruth 1:9, Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” A new husband and a home where they can rest. That's her send-off for both of them.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: Exactly, baker. Orpah and Ruth tell her, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) Naomi kisses them goodbye, and both of them answer, we're coming with you. That is not the answer she asked for.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: Nobody's waiting around, friend. Orpah and Ruth tell Naomi, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) They want to go WITH her, not wave from the porch. Two daughters-in-law, one answer, and it isn't goodbye.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: They're not promising a visit someday, baker. Orpah and Ruth tell her, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) That's not 'we should get together sometime,' the thing everybody says and nobody ever puts on the calendar. That's packing up and walking.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi asks, “would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands?” Even in her best-case picture, those sons would be newborns. She's doing the math for them, and the math is LONG.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: That's not her question, friend. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi asks, “would you wait for them to grow up?” Picture waiting on a husband who hasn't even been born yet. That's longer than anybody has ever sat on hold with the cable company.

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't sending anybody ahead, baker. In Ruth 1:13 she asks, “would you wait for them to grow up?” Then she adds, “Would you refrain from having husbands?” She's showing them how long that wait would be.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi says, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” That's how she sees everything she has lost. It's honest, and it's heavy.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: Naomi doesn't blame the people of Judah, friend. She isn't even back there yet. In Ruth 1:13 she says, “it is much more bitter for me than for you, because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” She points to the LORD, not to any people.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: She doesn't say a word against the people of Moab, baker. Her daughters-in-law are from Moab, and she just blessed them (Ruth 1:8-9). In Ruth 1:13 Naomi says it's bitter for her because the hand of the LORD has gone out against her. That's where she's pointing.

True, baker. Ruth 1:14 says, “Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye…” She heads back, just like Naomi kept asking. Hold that thought, because the other daughter-in-law is about to do something very different.
It's actually true, friend. Ruth 1:14 says, “Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye…” Naomi had told them to go home three times by now (Ruth 1:8, 11, 12). Orpah takes her up on it.
Ruth stays, baker. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, “but Ruth clung to her.” Orpah takes the road home, and Ruth holds on tight. Same road, two daughters-in-law, two different directions.

That's right, friend. Ruth 1:14 says Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, “but Ruth clung to her.” Ruth isn't going anywhere except wherever Naomi goes. I've seen chocolate chips hold on to warm dough with less commitment than that.

True, baker. In Ruth 1:15, Naomi says, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” That's her fourth try at sending them home (Ruth 1:8, 11, 12, 15). She's like an alarm that keeps going off no matter how many times you hit snooze.

It's actually true, friend. In Ruth 1:15, Naomi says, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” She's still trying to send Ruth back. But Ruth is about to give one of the most famous answers in the whole Bible.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. In Ruth 1:16, Ruth says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” She's not just changing her address. She's choosing Naomi's God.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: Ruth promises something bigger than chores, friend. In Ruth 1:16 she says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” Her promise goes past where she'll live to who her God will be. That's not a roommate agreement.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's not in her promise, baker. In Ruth 1:16, Ruth says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” She isn't signing up for a class on local customs. She's tying her whole life to Naomi and to Naomi's God.

That's the word, baker. In Ruth 1:17, Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” She calls on the LORD by name to hold her to it. That's as serious as a promise gets.

Distance isn't going to separate them, friend, because Ruth says wherever Naomi goes, she will go (Ruth 1:16). In Ruth 1:17 she says nothing but death will separate them. She puts the LORD's name on that promise. You cannot out-walk a woman like that.

Ruth doesn't name marriage, baker. In Ruth 1:17 she says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” Naomi kept bringing up new husbands (Ruth 1:9, 11-13). Ruth's answer leaves no wiggle room at all.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, “she stopped trying to persuade her.” Four tries, and she finally sets the argument down. Sometimes the one who wins is the one who simply will not leave.

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: She already tried that, friend, back in Ruth 1:15. After Ruth's promise, Ruth 1:18 says Naomi “stopped trying to persuade her.” No more sending anybody anywhere. Ruth said her piece, and Naomi lets it stand.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Nobody's waiting in Moab, baker. Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her. So they keep going together. Ruth 1:19 says they traveled until they came to Bethlehem.

That's it, baker. Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” She's been gone a long time (Ruth 1:4). It's like spotting an old coworker in the grocery line and going, wait, is that YOU?

They don't ask that, friend. Ruth 1:19 says the whole town was stirred, and the women exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” Naomi is the one who talks about what she's lost, right after (Ruth 1:20-21). The town's first words are just her name.

They're asking about Naomi, not Ruth, baker. Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” Ruth the Moabitess is right there with her (Ruth 1:22). But the town's eyes are on the one who came home.

Right, baker. In Ruth 1:20, Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi,” and then she says, “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” She gives her reason right there. That's a hard thing to hear from someone coming home.

Hannah is a different woman, friend, the mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 1:20). Here in Ruth 1:20, Naomi says, “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” She doesn't want to be called Naomi anymore. Mara is the name she asks for.

Leah is Jacob's wife over in Genesis (Genesis 29:23). In Ruth 1:20, Naomi tells the women of Bethlehem, “Call me Mara…” And she gives her reason: the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with her. New name, same Naomi, carrying a lot.

It's the other way around, baker. In Ruth 1:21, Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” She left with a husband and two sons, and she came back without them. I think every word of that one was hard to say.

Exactly, friend. In Ruth 1:21, Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” She left Bethlehem with her husband and her two sons (Ruth 1:1-2). Now she's back without them, and she says so plainly.

There it is, baker. Ruth 1:22 says Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem “at the beginning of the barley harvest.” The chapter opened with a famine (Ruth 1:1), and it closes with a harvest starting. Talk about walking in right as the oven timer goes off.

Not wheat this time, friend. Ruth 1:22 says they arrived “at the beginning of the barley harvest.” Barley is the word the verse uses. After a famine at the start of the chapter (Ruth 1:1), the fields are coming in.

No olives in this verse, baker. Ruth 1:22 says Naomi and Ruth arrived at the beginning of the barley harvest. The chapter started with a famine back in Ruth 1:1. Now the fields around Bethlehem are ready to be gathered.
